name: THE HOLLANDAISE RO-O-OH-O-OH-O-OH-OH-OH-OLL BURGER (comes with hollandaise sauce on a Kaiser roll)

recipe.history:
Hollandaise sauce is one of the five French mother sauces codified by Auguste Escoffier in his foundational culinary text Le Guide Culinaire (1903), though its origins are considerably older and more contested than its official classification suggests. The sauce — a warm emulsion of egg yolks, clarified butter, and lemon juice or white wine vinegar — almost certainly predates its French classification by centuries, appearing in Dutch and German cooking in various forms before French chefs claimed it and made it their own. The name 'hollandaise' is itself a nod to the Dutch, reflecting French acknowledgment of the Netherlands as the source of the exceptional butter that makes the sauce possible: Dutch butter was famous across Europe for its richness and quality, a product of the Holstein-Friesian cattle bred in the flat, fertile lowlands of Holland. The sauce appears in a 1758 French cookbook under a different name but essentially the same technique, and by the nineteenth century it was a fixture of French haute cuisine, appearing over asparagus, artichokes, poached fish, and eventually the eggs Benedict that became its most famous American context. The Kaiser roll — kaisersemmel in German — has its own history, originating in Vienna in the seventeenth or eighteenth century (the exact date is debated) and named, according to legend, in honor of Emperor Franz Joseph I. The roll's characteristic five-pointed star-shaped top, created by a specific folding technique, and its crisp crust with a slightly chewy interior made it the definitive roll of Viennese bakeries and eventually a standard bun for sandwiches and burgers across Central Europe and the United States.

Hollandaise on a burger in America is an extension of the eggs Benedict tradition, which itself became an American brunch institution in the twentieth century — associated with lazy Sunday mornings, bottomless mimosas, and the particular luxury of someone else making you a complicated sauce while you sit and wait. The idea of pairing this most indulgent of sauces with a burger is a declaration of no restraint whatsoever: butter on top of fat on top of beef, a stack of richness that only makes sense if every element is executed correctly. The Kaiser roll is not an accidental choice — its structure is capable of standing up to the liquid weight of hollandaise without immediately disintegrating, and its slightly yeasty, slightly tangy flavor holds its own against the butteriness of the sauce. Burger chefs began experimenting with hollandaise in the 2010s as brunch culture — and its attendant expectation of eggs and butter in every format — merged with craft burger culture in American cities.

I made hollandaise on a burger for the first time for a brunch gathering when I was showing off. I had made hollandaise for eggs Benedict dozens of times and knew the sauce by feel — when the yolks had thickened to ribbon stage, when the butter was going in too fast, the moment when everything was about to break and could be saved with a cold teaspoon of water. I made a double batch, cooked four patties in cast iron to a precise medium rare, and assembled the burgers on freshly baked Kaiser rolls that were still faintly warm. I spooned the hollandaise over the patties the way you would pour it over an English muffin — generously, without apology. People at the table went quiet. One person asked if it was legal. I said I didn't see why it wouldn't be.

Hollandaise is, metabolically speaking, a sauce made almost entirely of fat — butter fat and egg yolk fat — and its richness is its defining quality. The only thing in the world that balances that richness at the patty level is a medium-rare beef burger, 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit, with its pink, juicy interior and the faint mineral tang that properly cooked medium-rare ground beef carries. A well-done patty under hollandaise is a fat-on-fat collision with no contrast, no brightness, no point. The medium-rare patty provides the beefy, slightly mineral edge that cuts through the sauce's softness, the same way a perfectly poached egg's yolk provides a bright, eggy contrast to hollandaise in eggs Benedict. At 130–135°F, the burger makes sense. It is the only temperature at which it does.
ingredients: 1 tbsp white vinegar (for characteristic Kaiser tang)
poppy seeds or sesame seeds for topping
1 tbsp fresh lemon juice, plus more to taste
4 slices Canadian bacon or thick-cut ham, pan-seared
4 poached eggs (optional but traditional — this is a brunch burger)
fresh chives, finely chopped, for garnish
instructions: 1. Make the Kaiser rolls: In a large bowl, combine warm water, sugar, and yeast; rest 5 minutes until foamy. Add oil, white vinegar, bread flour, and salt. Knead on a lightly floured surface for 10 minutes until smooth and elastic. The dough will be somewhat firm. Place in an oiled bowl, cover, and rise 1 hour until doubled.

2. Divide dough into 4 equal portions. Shape each into a smooth ball. To create the Kaiser roll's characteristic star pattern: flatten each ball slightly and use kitchen scissors or a Kaiser roll stamp to cut 5 evenly spaced cuts from the center outward (like a pinwheel), each about halfway to the edge. Pinch and fold each section in sequence to create the characteristic swirl. Alternatively, simply shape into smooth round rolls. Place on a parchment-lined baking sheet, cover, and proof 30–40 minutes. Brush with egg white wash. Sprinkle with poppy or sesame seeds. Bake at 400°F (205°C) for 18–20 minutes until deep golden and the crust feels firm. Cool on a rack.

3. Clarify the butter: Melt 225g unsalted butter in a small saucepan over medium-low heat. The milk solids will sink and the white foam will rise. Skim the foam with a spoon. Carefully pour the clear yellow butterfat into a heatproof measuring cup or pitcher, leaving the white milk solids at the bottom. You should have approximately 175–190ml of clarified butter. Keep warm but not hot.

4. Make the hollandaise: In a medium heatproof bowl (or the top of a double boiler), combine egg yolks, cold water, lemon juice, and white wine vinegar. Set over a saucepan of barely simmering water — the bowl should not touch the water. Whisk vigorously and continuously for 3–5 minutes until the mixture thickens to ribbon stage — it should fall in thick ribbons when the whisk is lifted and doubled in volume.

5. Remove the bowl from the heat. Very slowly — drop by drop at first — begin adding the warm clarified butter, whisking constantly. As the emulsion establishes, you can begin pouring in a thin, steady stream. Continue adding butter until all of it is incorporated and the sauce is thick, glossy, and pale yellow. Season with cayenne, white pepper, and salt. Adjust lemon juice to taste. If the sauce is too thick, whisk in a teaspoon of warm water. Keep warm in the bowl set over the pot of warm (not simmering) water, whisking occasionally.
6. Sear the Canadian bacon: In a skillet over medium-high heat, sear Canadian bacon or ham slices 1–2 minutes per side until lightly browned and heated through. Set aside.

7. If including poached eggs: Fill a deep saucepan with 3 inches of water and bring to a gentle simmer. Add a splash of white vinegar. Crack each egg into a small cup. Create a gentle swirl in the water and slide each egg in. Poach 3–4 minutes until the whites are fully set but the yolks are still runny. Remove with a slotted spoon onto a paper towel. Season with salt.

8. Form the patties: Divide ground beef into 4 equal portions (about 175g each). Form into patties 4 inches wide and 3/4 inch thick, pressing a center dimple. Season generously with salt, pepper, and garlic powder just before cooking.

9. Cook the patties: Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until very hot. Add a thin film of neutral oil. Sear patties without moving for 3 minutes. Flip once. Cook 2 more minutes. Target internal temperature: 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare. Rest 3 minutes.
10. Split and lightly toast the Kaiser rolls cut-side down in the skillet 60–90 seconds.

11. Assemble: Place a leaf of butter lettuce and a tomato slice on the bottom roll. Place the medium-rare patty on top. Lay a slice of seared Canadian bacon on the patty. If using, gently place a poached egg on the Canadian bacon. Spoon hollandaise sauce generously over the entire stack — let it run freely down the sides. Scatter capers and fresh chives over the hollandaise. Place the top Kaiser roll on carefully and serve immediately, with extra hollandaise on the side.
